L2317@P54: TESTING LINEAR SPECTRAL UNMIXING ON LABORATORY MIXTURES: APPLICATION TO VIR DATA FOR
L2322@P54: C.A. Raymond, NASA/Jet Propulsion Laboratory and California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
L2323@P54: Abstract : At 525 km in mean diameter, Vesta is the second largest object of the main asteroid belt. The Visible and
L2324@P54: InfraRed (VIR) spectrometer onboard Dawn provided more than 20 millions spectra at variable spatial resolution, allowing one
L2325@P54: to discriminate the different lithologies on Vesta. In this work, we tested linear spectral unmixing on three different mixtures, to
L2326@P54: verify the applicability of linear unmixing to VIR data of Vesta, and to determine the accuracy of the detection of the amount of
L2327@P54: the different minerals. We studied the following mixtures: two pyroxenes, pyroxene and olivine, and pyroxene and plagioclase. We
L2328@P54: next applied linear spectral unmixing to VIR spectra for localized features and larger areas, with the goal of deriving the composition and abundance of the minerals present.
L2329@P54: A PRELIMINARY RESEARCH ON QUANTITATIVE RETRIEVAL OF HYDROUS MINERALS AROUND THE MARS
L2330@P54: SCIENCE LABORATORY LANDING SITE
L2331@P54: Tong Shuai and Xia Zhang, State Key Laboratory of Remote Sensing Sciences, Institute of Remote Sensing and Digital
L2332@P54: Earth, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100101, China
L2333@P54: Abstract : The detection of hydrous minerals is of great importance in revealing the early water environment and even
L2334@P54: biotic activities on Mars. However, few studies focus on quantitatively retrieving hydrous minerals due to some problems. In this
L2335@P54: paper, the area around the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) landing site is studied for quantitatively retrieving hydrous minerals.
L2336@P54: Firstly, the distribution of hydrous minerals is extracted using water absorption features. Then, sparse unmixing is employed with
L2337@P54: CRISM spectral library to retrieve the abundance of hydrous minerals in the hydrous region. The results show that seven hydrous
L2338@P54: minerals are quantitatively retrieved, e.g. actinolite, montmorillonite, saponite, jarosite and so forth, and the total concentration
L2339@P54: of all hydrous minerals can reach up to 40% near the lower reaches of Mount Sharp.

L2341@P54: NONLINEAR UNMIXING OF VEGETATED AREAS: A MODEL COMPARISON BASED ON SIMULATED AND REAL
L2342@P54: HYPERSPECTRAL DATA
L2343@P54: Nicolas Dobigeon, University of Toulouse, IRIT/INP-ENSEEIHT/TéSA, Toulouse, France

L2347@P54: School of Engineering and Physical Sciences, Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, U.K.
L2348@P54: Pol Coppin, Department of Biosystems, KU Leuven, Belgium
L2349@P54: Abstract : When analyzing remote sensing hyperspectral images, numerous works dealing with spectral unmixing assume the pixels result from linear combinations of the endmember signatures. However, this assumption cannot be fulfilled, in
L2350@P54: particular when considering images acquired over vegetated areas. As a consequence, several nonlinear mixing models have been
L2351@P54: recently derived to take various nonlinear effects into account when unmixing hyperspectral data. Unfortunately, these models
L2352@P54: have been empirically proposed and without thorough validation. This paper attempts to fill this gap by taking advantage of two
L2353@P54: sets of real and physical-based simulated data. The accuracy of various linear and nonlinear models and the corresponding unmixing algorithms is evaluated with respect to their ability of fitting the sensed pixels and of providing accurate estimates of the
L2354@P54: abundances.

L2364@P55: C. Louis, THALES Communications & Security, France
L2365@P55: Abstract : Rare endmembers estimation is a very interesting and difficult issue in the unmixing field. We focus on the
L2366@P55: case of a rare endmember which appear as a change between two images of a same scene. We use both the information of the
L2367@P55: image where the new endmember is missing and change detection results to estimate the appearing endmember. We base the proposed approach on spectral unmixing with non negative matrix factorization (NMF), adding appropriate constraints on changed
L2368@P55: or non-changed pixels. We choose to test and discuss the alternate projected gradient optimization scheme. We compare the
L2369@P55: results to those of the estimation of appearing endmember through classical NMF unmixing on simulated data.
L2370@P55: SPECTRAL-SPATIAL JOINT SPARSITY UNMIXING OF HYPERSPECTRAL DATA USING OVERCOMPLETE DICTIONARIES
L2371@P55: J. Bieniarz, E. Aguilera, X. X. Zhu, R. Müller, U. Heiden and P. Reinartz,
L2372@P55: German Aerospace Center (DLR), Oberpfaffenhofen, 82234 Wessling, Germany
L2373@P55: Abstract : Sparse spectral unmixing can be modeled as a linear combination of endmembers contained in an overcomplete dictionary weighted by the corresponding sparse abundance vector. This method exploits the fact that there is only a small
L2374@P55: number of endmembers inside a pixel compared to the overcomplete endmember spectral dictionary. Since the information contained in hyperspectral pixels is often spatially correlated, in this work we propose to jointly estimate the sparse abundance vectors
L2375@P55: of neighboring hyperspectral pixels within a local window exploiting joint sparsity with common and noncommon endmembers.
L2376@P55: To demonstrate the efficiency of our framework, we perform experiments using both simulated and real hyperspectral data.
L2377@P55: A ROBUST SUBSPACE METHOD FOR SEMIBLIND DICTIONARY-AIDED HYPERSPECTRAL UNMIXING
L2378@P55: Xiao Fu and Wing-Kin Ma, Dept. Electronic Eng., The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shatin, N.T., Hong Kong
L2379@P55: José M. Bioucas-Dias, Instituto de Telecomunicações and Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisboa, Portugal
L2380@P55: Tsung-Han Chan, Sunplus Technology Co., Hsinchu, Taiwan
L2381@P55: Abstract : Recent development in semiblind dictionary-aided hyperspectral unmixing (HU) shows that a classical
L2382@P55: method in sensor array processing, namely, multiple signal classification (MUSIC), provides an effective way for endmember
L2383@P55: identification. However, MUSIC (and in fact, other dictionary-based sparse regression algorithms) assumes that there are no mismatches between the true endmember signatures and the dictionary spectral signatures, which may be violated in practice owing
L2384@P55: to reasons such as endmember variability and calibration errors. This paper presents a robust MUSIC method, wherein spectral
L2385@P55: signature mismatches are incorporated in the original MUSIC formulation to make the resulting algorithm robust. A computationally simple method is derived for the implementation of robust MUSIC. Simulation results show that robust MUSIC provides
L2386@P55: improved robustness against spectral signature mismatches than the original MUSIC.
L2387@P55: ESTIMATION OF NUMBER OF SIGNAL SUBSPACES IN HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGERY USING LOW-RANK SUBSPACE REPRESENTATION
L2388@P55: Alex Sumarsono and Qian Du, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Mississippi State University, USA
L2389@P55: Abstract : In this paper, we address the problem of hyperspectral subspace estimation based on low-rank representation.
L2390@P55: It is often assumed that major signal sources occupy a low-rank subspace. Due to the mixed nature of hyperspectral data, the underlying data structure may include multiple subspaces instead of a single subspace. Therefore, in this paper, we propose the use
L2391@P55: of low-rank subspace representation to estimate the number of subspaces. In particular, we develop simple estimation approaches
L2392@P55: without user-defined parameters. Real data experiments demonstrate excellent performance of the proposed approaches.

L2404@P56: Abstract : In this contribution measurements of the Airborne Prism Experiment (APEX) imaging spectrometer were
L2405@P56: used to derive products related to plant traits, e.g., leaf chlorophyll, carotenoid, anthocyanin, and water content, leaf greenness,
L2406@P56: biomass, and leaf area index. The Apex products were highly correlated to the related ground truth measurements in major crops
L2407@P56: under experimental and field situations. The relationship of APEX derived NDVI (NDVIAPEX) with ground measured NDVI and
L2408@P56: canopy cover is shown in detail. Additionally, interrelations between the aerial detected traits are discussed. The combination of
L2409@P56: the presented remotely measured plant traits can potentially give crop specific indications of their growth status and vitality. Such
L2410@P56: tools could help to improve resource use efficiency in agricultural systems and are needed for applications in precision agriculture
L2411@P56: and mapping of land use and land cover for scientific purposes or decision making.
L2412@P56: ESTIMATING BIOMASS OF RICE IN FARMERS’ FIELDS BY RED-EDGE INDICES
L2413@P56: Martin Leon Gnyp and Kang Yu, Institute of Geography, GIS & RS group, University of Cologne, Cologne, Germany
L2414@P56: International Center for Agro-Informatics and Sustainable Development, ICASD
L2415@P56: Yuxin Miao, College of Resources and Environmental Sciences, China Agricultural University, Beijing, China
L2416@P56: International Center for Agro-Informatics and Sustainable Development, ICASD
L2417@P56: Georg Bareth, Institute of Geography, GIS & RS group, University of Cologne, Cologne, Germany
L2418@P56: International Center for Agro-Informatics and Sustainable Development, ICASD
L2419@P56: Abstract : Biomass is an important parameter that has a decisive influence on the final yield. Destructive measurements
L2420@P56: of biomass are time-consuming and labor-intensive. Proximal sensing methods using field spectrometers offer indirect observation and estimation of biomass. For this purpose, farmers’ fields were investigated in a two-year growing season of rice and canopy
L2421@P56: reflectance was measured by spectrometers. Several vegetation indices (VIs) and multiple linear regression (MLR) models based
L2422@P56: on bands around the red-edge domain (680-760 nm) were tested. Published red- edge VIs were generally prone to saturation,
L2423@P56: whereas MLR models and the Ratio of Reflectance Difference Index in the red-edge (RRDIre) were less influenced by saturation.
L2424@P56: The linearly tested MLR (based on VIs) and the RRDIre models provided the best performance for biomass estimation in model
L2425@P56: validation using an independent dataset.
L2426@P56: HYPERSPECTRAL TREE SPECIES CLASSIFICATION WITH AN AID OF LIDAR DATA
L2427@P56: Tomohiro Matsuki, Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, The University of Tokyo
L2428@P56: Naoto Yokoya and Akira Iwasaki, Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology, The University of Tokyo
L2429@P56: Abstract : Classification of tree species is one of the most important applications in remote sensing. A methodology to
L2430@P56: classify tree species using hyperspectral and LiDAR data is proposed. The data processing consists of shadow correction, individual tree crown delineation, classification by support vector machine (SVM) and postprocessing by a smoothing filter. The authors
L2431@P56: applied this procedure to the data taken over Tama Forest Science Garden in Tokyo, Japan and classified it into 16 classes of tree
L2432@P56: species. As a result, the authors achieved classification accuracy of 79 % with 10 % training data, which is 17 % higher than what
L2433@P56: is obtained by using hyperspectral data only. Shadow correction and morphological processing derived from LiDAR data increase
L2434@P56: the accuracy by 3 % and 14 %, respectively.

L2438@P57: SPECTRAL DISCRIMINATION OF TEA PLANT VARIETIES BY STATISTICAL, MACHINE LEARNING AND SPECTRAL SIMILARITY METHODS
L2439@P57: Rama Rao Nidamanuri,
L2440@P57: Department of Earth and Space Sciences, Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, Thiruvananthapuram, India
L2441@P57: Abstract : Remote discrimination and mapping of tea plantations is a valuable tool for efficient management of inventory
L2442@P57: and optimization of resources. Apart from the planting multiple tea varieties, growth of natural vegetation species is common
L2443@P57: scenario in plantations. The objective of this research was spectral discrimination of nine important tea varieties in the presence
L2444@P57: of six natural vegetation species in Munnar, Western Ghat highlands of south India. Discrimination models using six methods: knearest neighborhood classifier (k-NN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), support vector machines (SVM), normalized spectral
L2445@P57: similarity score (NS3), maximum likelihood classifier (MLC) and artificial neural networks (ANNs) were applied on the hyperspectral reflectance measurements collected at canopy level. The existence and statistical significance of spectral differences of the
L2446@P57: tea and natural vegetation species were assessed by MANOVA. Results indicate that six out of 9 tea varieties could be discriminated with best accuracies 75 to 80%. While a closer spectral similarity is observed in few tea varieties, the presence of natural
L2447@P57: vegetation species has decreased inter species variability for few tea varieties while enhancing the same for few other tea varieties
L2448@P57: at the cost of reducing spectral separability among the vegetation species.
L2449@P57: TOWARDS ROBUST VEGETATION INDICES: THE MULTI-CORRELATION MATRIX STRATEGY
L2450@P57: Helge Aasen, Institute of Geography, GIS & RS group, University of Cologne, Cologne, Germany

L2458@P57: Abstract : This paper presents a new fusion approach producing unobservable fused remote sensing data with high spatial and spectral resolutions. This approach, related to linear spectral unmixing (LSU) techniques, introduces joint nonnegative
L2459@P57: matrix factorization (JNMF) for combining observable low spatial resolution hyperspectral and high spatial resolution multispectral data. JNMF is applied to synthetic but realistic data generated from real airborne hyperspectral data. Spectral and spatial
L2460@P57: qualities of fused data are evaluated by frequently used criteria. Experimental results show the low computational cost of the proposed approach, and the good spectral and spatial fidelities of the fused data. Our method also outperforms the recently proposed
L2461@P57: coupled nonnegative matrix factorization (CNMF) method.

L2463@P57: GEOMETRIC MATCHED FILTER FOR HYPERSPECTRAL PARTIAL UNMIXING
L2464@P57: Muhammad Awais Akhter, Rob Heylen and Paul Scheunders,
L2465@P57: iMinds-Vision Lab, Department of Physics, University of Antwerp, Belgium
L2466@P57: Abstract : In this paper, a new geometric matched filter is presented by combining the standard matched filtering with
L2467@P57: concepts of convex geometry. The purpose of the method is partial unmixing of a hyperspectral image, where an estimate is given
L2468@P57: for the relative contribution of each pixel to a specific target spectrum. In standard matched filtering, the filter is designed based
L2469@P57: on the background statistics of the entire image, which works fine when the target is contained in a limited number of pixels, but
L2470@P57: fails when the target is abundantly present throughout the whole image. The presented method calculates the filter based on the
L2471@P57: statistics of pixels that do not contain the target spectrum. These background pixels are identified based on the simplex formed
L2472@P57: by the target and other relevant endmembers of the dataset. In the experiments, the presented method is shown to outperform
L2473@P57: standard matched filtering for partial unmixing.

L2489@P58: Abstract : In this paper, we present a new maximum distance method (MDM) by applying the simplex barycentric coordinate for endmember extraction, named BC-MDM. Under linear mixing model and pure-pixel assumption, the MDM, which
L2490@P58: is proposed by Geng in 2005, is based on the fact that a pixel is an endmember if it has the maximum distance to the sub-simplex
L2491@P58: with vertices being endmembers already extracted. Calculating the distance of a pixel to the sub-simplex is quite time-consuming.
L2492@P58: To overcome this problem, we introduce the idea of barycentric coordinate to MDM, which transforms the problem of distance
L2493@P58: calculation into spectral unmixing with abundance sum-to-one constraint. As a result, BC-MDM has greatly reduced the computational complexity of original MDM. The experimental results with real hyperspectral image demonstrate that compared to
L2494@P58: the simplex growing algorithm (SGA), the proposed method can provide the same performance with a computational complexity between one and two orders magnitude lower, and compared to vertex component analysis (VCA), our method can provide
L2495@P58: consistent result while requires less computing time.
L2496@P58: Combining Multi-Agent and Ant Colony Optimization for Endmember Extraction
L2497@P58: Lina Yang, Xu Sun, Qian Shen, Bing Zhang and Tianhe Chi
L2498@P58: Chinese Academy of Sciences Institute of Remote Sensing and Digital Earth Beijing, China
L2499@P58: Abstract : Ant colony optimization (ACO) is an effective algorithm to extracting endmembers in the field of hyperspectral remote sensing. However, its speed is relatively low, and the increasing data size will cause its decreasing computing efficiency.
L2500@P58: Based on Agent-Oriented Programming paradigm to build a distributed Multi-Agent System (MAS) of ACO to extract endmembers is an efficient way of reducing computing time. By designing a distributed architecture that consists of a manager agent and
L2501@P58: multiple ant agents, and assigning agents different behaviors and communication contents, this paper proposes and realizes an
L2502@P58: ACO and MAS combined method to make ants execute endmember extraction tasks in parallel. Moreover, three comparative
L2503@P58: experiments using an AVIRIS image have been done to test the method, which proves that using multiple hosts to build MAS can
L2504@P58: greatly improve the efficiency of intelligent computing.
L2505@P58: AN IMPROVED WEIGHT-CALCULATION NON-LOCAL SPARSE UNMIXING FOR HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGERY
L2506@P58: Ruyi Feng, Yanfei Zhong and Liangpei Zhang
L2507@P58: State Key Laboratory of Information Engineering in Surveying, Mapping, and Remote Sensing, Wuhan University, P. R. China
L2508@P58: Abstract : Spatial sparse unmixing techniques have been known as a series of effective way in improving the unmixing
L2509@P58: accuracy with the integration of spatial correlations of imagery. To better utilize the non-local spatial information, spatial sparse
L2510@P58: unmixing methods based on non-local means such as non- local sparse unmixing (NLSU) have been proposed. However, the
L2511@P58: non-local spatial correlations in NLSU represented by weights between similar windows in the estimated abundances are always
L2512@P58: changing and not so reliable during the process of optimization. To obtain more precise and fixed spatial relationships, the improved weight- calculation non-local sparse unmixing algorithm is proposed in this paper by replacing the weight acquisition
L2513@P58: source from the variable estimated abundances to original hyperspectral imagery. The experimental results using two groups of
L2514@P58: simulated hyperspectral datasets indicate that the IW-NLSU outperforms the previous spatial sparse unmixing methods.

L2520@P59: STRUCTURED SPARSE BAYESIAN HYPERSPECTRAL COMPRESSIVE SENSING USING SPECTRAL UNMIXING
L2521@P59: Lei Zhang, Wei Wei, Yanning Zhang, Fei Li and Hangqi Yan
L2522@P59: School of Computer Science, Northwestern Polytechnical University, Xian, China
L2523@P59: Abstract : To reduce huge consumption of processing hyperspectral images(HSI), a novel Bayesian unmixing compressive
L2524@P59: sensing framework is proposed to compress and reconstruct HSI effectively, called structured sparse Bayesian umixing compressive
L2525@P59: sensing(SSBUCS). SSBUCS unites compressive sensing and hyperspectral linear mixed model in Bayesian framework. An HSI is
L2526@P59: decomposed as a linear combination of endmembers and abundance matrix. The abundance matrix is transformed to a structured
L2527@P59: sparse signal in the wavelet domain. Then, compressive sensing is employed on this sparse signal to produce a more compact result.
L2528@P59: To recover the HSI, a Markov chain Monte Carlo(MCMC) method based on Gibbs sampling is proposed, imposing structured sparse
L2529@P59: prior on abundance matrix. Experimental results verify the superiority of the proposed method over several state-of-art methods.
L2530@P59: Sparse unmixing via WM algorithm for hyperspectral images
L2531@P59: Ion Marques Student Member, IEEE, and Manuel Graña Member, IEEE
L2532@P59: Abstract : Spectral unmixing aims to estimate the fractional abundances of spectral signatures in each pixel. The Linear Mixing Model (LMM) of hyperspectral images assumes that pixel spectra are affine combinations of fundamental spectral signatures called
L2533@P59: endmembers. Endmember induction algorithms (EIA) extract the endmembers from the hyperspectral data. The WM algorithm assumes that a set of Affine Independent vectors can be extracted from the rows and columns of dual Lattice Autoassociative Memories
L2534@P59: (LAAM) built on the image spectra. Indeed, the set of endmembers induced by this algorithm defines a convex polytope covering the
L2535@P59: hyperspectral image data. However, the number of endmembers extracted can be huge. This calls for additional endmember selection
L2536@P59: steps, and to approaching the unmixing problem with linear sparse regression techniques. In this paper, we combine WM algorithm
L2537@P59: with clustering techniques and Conjugate Gradient Pursuit (CGP) for endmember induction. Our experiments are conducted using
L2538@P59: hyperspectral imaging obtained by the Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectometer of the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
L2539@P59: ENDMEMBER CONSTRAINED SEMI-SUPERVISED HYPERSPECTRAL UNMIXING
L2540@P59: Jakob Sigurdsson, Magnus O. Ulfarsson and Johannes R. Sveinsson, University of Iceland, Dept. Electrical Eng., Reykjavik, Iceland
L2541@P59: Abstract : In this paper an endmember constrained semi-supervised hyperspectral unmixing method is proposed. The
L2542@P59: linear model is used to represent the hyperspectral data. A priori information about the endmembers is incorporated into the
L2543@P59: objective function with soft regularization. This information can be acquired from a spectral library or from the data itself. Quantitative evaluation of the method is done using simulated data and it is shown the soft regularization can yield better results than
L2544@P59: hard regularization. The method is also applied on a real hyperspectral data set and the estimated abundance maps improve when
L2545@P59: a priori information is used to aid the unmixing.
L2546@P59: VALIDATING NONLINEAR MIXING MODELS: BENCHMARK DATASETS FROM VEGETATED AREAS
L2547@P59: L. Tits, KU Leuven - Dept. of biosystems, Geomatics Lab, BE-3001 Leuven, Belgium
L2548@P59: B. Somers, KU Leuven - Division Forest, Nature and Landscape, BE-3001 Leuven, Belgium
L2549@P59: J. Stuckens, Merkator NV, BE-1731 Zellik, Belgium
L2550@P59: P. Coppin, KU Leuven - Dept. of biosystems, Geomatics Lab, BE-3001 Leuven, Belgium
L2551@P59: Abstract : Our understanding of nonlinear mixing events in vegetated areas is currently hampered by a pertinent lack
L2552@P59: of well-validated datasets. Most quantification and modeling efforts are based on theoretical assumptions or indirect empirical
L2553@P59: observations. In this study, a physically based ray tracer was used to create simulated hyperspectral datasets of vegetative systems.
L2554@P59: This model incorporates multiple scattering effects, and nonlinear mixing behavior can be observed in the rendered data. The
L2555@P59: main benefit of the ray-tracer is that we were able to demonstrate with in situ measurements that both the nature and the intensity
L2556@P59: of the nonlinear mixing events are realistically modeled. Different ray-tracer datasets will be made available to the wider scientific
L2557@P59: community as a benchmark dataset to test and validate new and existing unmixing methodologies. In this contribution, we would
L2558@P59: like to present the structure of these datasets, and show how they can be used to evaluate nonlinear mixing models. In addition,
L2559@P59: and maybe even more important, we would like to draw the attention to the limitations of the data, as well point out the assumptions made in the construction of the data.

L2571@P60: Abstract : Orthogonal vector projection (OVP) is recently developed as a versatile technique which can used in various application in hyperspectral imaging such as subpixel detection, linear spectral unmixing and endmember finding. A great
L2572@P60: advantage of OVP is that only calculations of vector products are required with no need of matrix multiplications and inverse
L2573@P60: calculations. Furthermore, this paper develops a recursive version of OVP, to be called recursive OVP (ROVP) so that OVP can
L2574@P60: be performed vector by vector recursively without using previously processed vectors. As a result, the computational complexity
L2575@P60: of ROVP is much lower than other algorithms. Furthermore, the ROVP is much easier to be applied to hardware such as FPGA
L2576@P60: or GPU in the future.
